Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette:
At 74, Minh Tran had spent most of his adult life in the United States, building a steady life with his wife and working as a welder, but the memories that brought him to treatment began much earlier, when he was a civilian in a war zone as a young man in Southeast Asia. He described one attack in particular that has never settled into a clear story. He remembers the sound first: engines and cars in the street, then noise, panic, people running, and the sudden sense that there was no safe place to stand in the open. What remains with him is fractured. He can recall pieces of what happened, but large parts feel missing, as if the middle has been torn out. At times the memory feels unreal even to him, too extreme to belong to his own life, and at other times it feels strangely alien, as though he is remembering something that happened to another man. Yet the gaps themselves have become meaningful to him. Minh has come to believe that if he had acted differently, moved sooner, chosen another place to stand, the event might not have unfolded as it did. The broken, dreamlike quality of the memory has not softened it; instead it leaves him fixed on the conviction that what happened was deeply unfair and that the people responsible were never held accountable.

Those beliefs have followed him for decades and shape how he moves through the present. He is certain that nothing was ever made right, and that sense of unresolved injustice keeps the danger feeling current rather than past. He lies awake for long stretches before sleep, feeling he must stay alert, as if letting his guard down would be foolish. During the day he notices how quickly his attention breaks apart, especially when there is noise around him. At the welding shop, the clatter of vehicles outside or the rev of a car in the lot can pull him out of what he is doing in an instant. He becomes watchful, scanning the space around him before he can return to the task in front of him. What frightens him most is how easily ordinary sounds are no longer ordinary; because he believes those who caused such harm were never stopped, part of him remains braced for danger to appear again.

The triggers are now woven into daily life. Car sounds are the strongest. If a vehicle backfires outside the shop or a car accelerates sharply on the street, the present loosens and the old scene presses forward in fragments: noise, exposure, confusion, missing pieces that he cannot organize. Sometimes even a spell of breathlessness, especially when he is exerting himself in a hot workspace with a welding mask on, jolts him into the same state. News footage or related war media can do it as well; a few seconds on television are enough to leave him unsettled for hours. Because these moments so often stir up those strange, partial recollections, he has become increasingly careful about what he allows himself to encounter. He changes the channel immediately, tells himself to think about something else, and avoids open or exposed spaces whenever he can. At work he prefers enclosed areas of the shop and dislikes stepping out into wide lots or open yards, where he feels too visible and unprotected.

Minh also avoids talking about the event, including with his wife. Part of him believes there is no point in talking because nothing can undo what happened and no one was ever made to answer for it. Another part feels ashamed, because he still blames himself for the way he acted that day. When the memory comes in jagged, disconnected pieces, he tries to redirect his mind quickly, pushing it aside before it can gather force. But the less he says and the faster he turns away, the less coherent it seems to become. The story remains patchy and unreal, and that incompleteness leaves more room for self-blame and for the old sense that something terrible and unfinished is still hanging over him. He notices that after he has spent a day dodging the subject, avoiding open areas, and forcing his thoughts elsewhere, he is even more on edge by nightfall.

Over the past year the cycle has tightened. Poor sleep leaves him more watchful the next day, and in that keyed-up state he catches every engine noise and every change in his breathing. Once triggered, his concentration drops, his body stays tense, and he becomes more determined to shut the whole thing down by not talking and by mentally steering away from it. His wife has told him he seems far away, especially in the evenings when the television is on and he insists on avoiding any war-related program without explaining why. He finally agreed to seek help after realizing he was structuring more and more of his workday and home life around not being caught off guard. What he fears is that if he stops avoiding it, the memory will become overwhelming; what he hopes, quietly, is that it might finally begin to feel like something that happened in his life rather than something broken, unfinished, and still waiting outside.
